The thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus) exhibited a suite of reproductive and life-history traits that were distinctive among large-bodied marsupial carnivores. Gestation in this species was brief, lasting approximately 30 days [tg = approximately 30 days] under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the pouch environment, which is maintained at a stable temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]. This short gestation period is consistent with the general pattern among dasyurid and thylacinid marsupials, where a rudimentary altricial young is born after a minimal uterine development phase. The wet weight at birth for the thylacine neonate was remarkably small, estimated at only 0.2 grams [Wwb = 0.2 grams], a value that underscores the extreme altriciality of the newborn pup. Upon emergence from the birth canal, these tiny offspring would crawl into the mother's pouch, where they would attach to a teat and continue their development, sustained entirely by milk during the subsequent weeks of pouch life.

Following parturition, the neonatal thylacine underwent a prolonged period of lactation and pouch dependency. The time since birth at weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence from milk, has been estimated at 16 weeks [tx = 16 weeks] under conditions of stable maternal body temperature (35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]). This duration of maternal investment meant that weaned juveniles began consuming solid food, likely small vertebrates and carrion brought to the den by the adult female, after roughly four months of postnatal care. The weaning period was followed by a lengthy juvenile phase during which the growing thylacine learned to hunt and navigate its territory. Females attained sexual maturity at a comparatively late age for a marsupial of this size; the time since birth at puberty for females has been estimated at 2 years [tp = 2 years] under typical thermal conditions of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], reflecting the extended development required before reproductive competence was achieved. This pattern of prolonged maternal care and delayed maturation is characteristic of apex predators that must acquire complex hunting skills before independence.

As adults, thylacines displayed notable sexual dimorphism in body size, a characteristic that likely influenced their respective ecological roles within the Tasmanian ecosystem. The ultimate wet weight for adult females, representing the maximum recorded body mass, reached approximately 25,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 25,000 grams], while males attained a substantially heavier ultimate wet weight of about 35,000 grams [Wwi = about 35,000 grams]. This pronounced disparity in mass, with males being roughly 40% heavier than females, is consistent with a polygynous or resource-defense mating system, where larger body size offers a competitive advantage in male-male contests over access to breeding females. In terms of skeletal dimension, the ultimate length from nose to tail base for males measured approximately 129.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 129.5 centimeters], providing a robust frame for the pursuit of medium-sized prey such as wallabies and wombats. This body plan, combining a relatively long, stiff tail with powerful limbs, conferred a distinctive loping gait well-suited for sustained pursuit through the forest understory.

The maximum longevity observed for Thylacinus cynocephalus, based on the oldest documented wild individuals and captive records, was approximately 12.7 years [am = approximately 12.7 years] at a temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]. This lifespan, recorded under the standard thermal conditions of the species' core body temperature at 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], positions the thylacine at the slower end of the life-history continuum for dasyuromorphs, comparable in duration to that of the Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii). The reproductive output of female thylacines was tuned to this relatively extended lifespan through a moderate fecundity strategy. Under stable maternal thermal conditions at 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], a receptive female would typically produce between 2 and 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 4 pups per litter], and field observations suggest that under favorable conditions, she could raise up to 2 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 2 litters per year]. This combined annual output constituted the maximum reproduction rate for the species, allowing a modest rate of population replacement in the stable, resource-rich habitats of pre-European Tasmania.

Comparative anatomical studies of the thylacine's skull and dentition have provided further insight into its ecological niche as an apex predator. The long, gape-limited jaws, containing more teeth than those of a canid of similar size, allowed the thylacine to deliver a precise, crushing bite to the base of a prey animal's skull. Analysis of dental microwear patterns suggests a dietary specialization on moderate-sized macropods, a hunting strategy that would have required substantial daily energy intake. Although direct metabolic measurements are unavailable for this extinct species, allometric scaling equations based on a body mass of 25 to 35 kilograms predict a basal metabolic rate consistent with that of a typical marsupial carnivore of equivalent size. The ecological role of the thylacine as the sole large mammalian predator in Tasmania prior to human arrival underscores the significance of its life-history parameters; the combination of a brief gestation and a lengthy period of maternal investment meant that population turnover rates were relatively slow, rendering the species especially vulnerable to the pressures of persecution and habitat fragmentation during the colonial era.
